observations.text: SP executed the entry in spin as briefed, but did not apply the recovery steps by heart, and the IP directed the sequence and made part of the control inputs. Level flight was regained 400 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, with the exit heading 15 degrees from the entry heading. Performance is within the standards expected for this stage, however it sits at the lower edge of them, since IP direction was required for every step and not only for the sequencing. Knowledge of the recovery procedures by heart is expected to remove the need for step-by-step direction on the next sortie.

SP recited the recovery procedures and made all the control inputs personally, needing only the IP's verbal prompts on the order of the steps, without any intervention on the controls. Stick movements were smooth and solid, and level flight was regained with the airspeed 20 knots from the target and the exit heading 10 degrees from the entry heading, the errors being recognized and corrected with delay. No secondary stall was allowed to appear and no A/C limit was exceeded. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP applied the Spin Recovery Procedures from memory, without the IP's verbal prompts or intervention, keeping the stick movements smooth and solid throughout. Minor errors in the timing of the pull-out produced a level-off 200 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and an exit heading 8 degrees from the entry heading, both recognized and corrected in a timely manner. No secondary stall appeared and no A/C limit was approached. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP knew the recovery procedures by heart and applied them promptly and accurately at the first indication of the spin, with smooth and solid stick movements. The A/C was recovered with minimum loss of altitude, level flight being regained within 100 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 8 knots of the target airspeed and within 4 degrees of the entry heading. No secondary stall was allowed to appear and all A/C limits were respected. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP applied the Spin Prevention and Spin Recovery Procedures from memory without hesitation, confirming the direction of rotation correctly on every entry. Stick movements were smooth, solid and free of over-control, and recovery was achieved with negligible loss of altitude, level flight being regained within 30 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 3 knots of the target airspeed and within 1 degree of the entry heading. No secondary stall developed at any point and the A/C limits were maintained with a wide margin. Accuracy and speed of execution were above the level expected of a student at this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a non-standardized application of the recovery sequence, did not neutralize the flight controls before confirming that the rotation had stopped, and could not complete the Spin Recovery Procedures without assistance. The IP directed the remaining steps and executed part of the control inputs, with the result that level flight was regained 500 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 18 degrees from the entry heading. Study of the recovery procedures to memory standard is required before the item is repeated.

SP, due to the startle effect at the onset of the departure from controlled flight, did not initiate the memorized recovery steps and made abrupt rather than smooth and solid stick movements. The IP had to take the controls to stop the rotation, with the result that the A/C was recovered 900 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 45 knots from the target airspeed and 30 degrees from the entry heading. A secondary stall was allowed to appear during the pull-out and the proper action was taken by the IP, not by the SP.

SP completed the Spin Recovery Procedures within the standards expected for this stage, requiring the IP's verbal prompts only for the confirmation of the direction of rotation, without intervention on the controls. Errors in the timing of the recovery inputs were recognized and corrected with delay, so level flight was regained 300 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 20 knots from the target airspeed and 10 degrees from the entry heading. Marginal performance for the Training Section - these values sit exactly on the limit of the acceptable band, and recall of the recovery procedures by heart is expected to reduce the prompting required on the next sortie.

SP applied the recovery procedures from memory and executed them without the IP's verbal prompts, with smooth and solid stick movements throughout. Minor errors in the rate of the pull-out produced a level-off 250 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and an exit heading 7 degrees from the entry heading, both recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention. No secondary stall was allowed to appear and no A/C limit was exceeded. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP knew the recovery procedures by heart and applied them promptly and accurately, with smooth and solid stick movements and no over-control in the pull-out. The A/C was recovered with minimum loss of altitude, level flight being regained within 120 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 7 knots of the target airspeed and within 4 degrees of the entry heading. No secondary stall appeared and the A/C limits were respected throughout. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP recited and applied the Spin Prevention and Spin Recovery Procedures without hesitation, identifying the direction of rotation correctly on every entry. Stick movements were smooth and solid, recovery was achieved with negligible loss of altitude, and level flight was regained within 40 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 3 knots of the target airspeed and within 2 degrees of the entry heading. No secondary stall developed and the A/C limits were maintained with a comfortable margin at all times. Accuracy and speed of execution were above the level expected at this point of the syllabus. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incorrect identification of the direction of rotation, applied the recovery inputs in the wrong sense and did not stop the rotation. The IP took the controls and completed the Spin Recovery Procedures, with the result that the A/C was recovered 800 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 30 degrees from the entry heading. The direction of rotation is to be confirmed against the flight instruments before any recovery input is made.

SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, did not know the recovery steps by heart and stopped the sequence after the first action. The IP directed the remaining steps and executed part of the control inputs, with the result that level flight was regained 600 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 35 knots from the target airspeed and 20 degrees from the entry heading. Further study of the spin prevention and spin recovery procedures is required before the item is repeated.

SP, due to an abrupt aft stick input during the pull-out, did not keep the stick movements smooth and solid and allowed a secondary stall to appear after the rotation had stopped. The condition was recognized and the proper action was taken only after the IP's verbal prompt, with the result that level flight was regained 300 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 20 knots from the target airspeed. No A/C limit was exceeded and the IP did not intervene on the controls.

SP, due to overconfidence in the margin available at that airspeed and bank, did not complete the spin prevention actions at the first indication of the departure and let the rotation develop. The recovery was then flown only after the IP's verbal prompts, and the errors in the sequence were recognized and corrected with delay, with the result that level flight was regained 300 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 10 degrees from the entry heading. No secondary stall appeared and the A/C limits were respected.

SP applied the Spin Recovery Procedures from memory within the desired standards, without the IP's verbal prompts or intervention. However, the pull-out was checked twice before level flight was established, so the A/C was recovered 290 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 19 knots from the target airspeed and 9 degrees from the entry heading. Marginal performance for the Training Section - the errors were self-corrected in a timely manner, and smoother, more solid stick movements in the pull-out are expected to bring these values well inside the desired band on the next sortie.

SP knew the recovery procedures by heart and applied them promptly and accurately at the first indication of the spin, with smooth and solid stick movements. The A/C was recovered with minimum loss of altitude, level flight being regained within 130 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 8 knots of the target airspeed and within 4 degrees of the entry heading. No secondary stall was allowed to appear and no A/C limit was approached. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP applied the Spin Prevention and Spin Recovery Procedures from memory without hesitation on every entry, identifying the direction of rotation correctly each time. Stick movements were smooth, solid and free of over-control, and recovery was achieved with negligible loss of altitude, level flight being regained within 40 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 3 knots of the target airspeed and within 2 degrees of the entry heading. No secondary stall developed and the A/C limits were maintained with a wide margin. Accuracy and speed of execution exceeded the level expected at the end of the block. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a delayed reduction of the power lever at the spin entry, did not arrest the rotation with the prescribed recovery inputs and could not complete the procedure without assistance. The IP took the controls to stop the rotation and complete the recovery, with the result that the A/C was recovered 850 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 40 degrees from the entry heading. A secondary stall appeared during the pull-out and the proper action was taken by the IP, not by the SP.

SP, due to a skill-based error in control input during the recovery, applied aileron against the direction of rotation instead of neutralizing the controls, and the rotation continued. The IP directed the correct inputs and executed part of the recovery, with the result that level flight was regained 700 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 40 knots from the target airspeed and 25 degrees from the entry heading. The A/C limits were not exceeded, but the item cannot be assessed as completed without assistance.

SP, due to an incomplete recall of the recovery steps, did not apply the procedure in the prescribed sequence and omitted the confirmation of the direction of rotation. The sequence was completed only after the IP's verbal prompts and the omission was recognized and corrected with delay, with the result that level flight was regained 300 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 10 degrees from the entry heading. No secondary stall appeared and no A/C limit was exceeded.

SP, due to an unmanaged stress response after the departure from controlled flight, did not carry out the recovery steps in the prescribed order and remained on the altimeter instead of confirming the direction of rotation. The sequence was completed after the IP's verbal prompts, with recognition and correction coming late, so level flight was regained 300 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 20 knots from the target airspeed and 10 degrees from the entry heading. The IP did not intervene on the controls and no A/C limit was exceeded.

SP, due to a late check of the pull-out at the completion of the rotation, did not recover the A/C with minimum loss of altitude and went through the briefed recovery altitude. The deviation was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention, with the result that level flight was established 250 feet below the briefed recovery altitude and 8 degrees from the entry heading. Stick movements remained smooth and solid and no secondary stall appeared.

SP, due to an interrupted cross-check of the aircraft state against the primary flight instruments once the rotation had stopped, did not capture the target airspeed at the end of the recovery. The error was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention, with the result that level flight was established 18 knots from the target airspeed and 200 feet below the briefed recovery altitude. No secondary stall was allowed to appear and no A/C limit was approached.

SP knew the recovery procedures by heart and applied them promptly and accurately, within the desired standards and without IP's intervention. However, the stick movements in the pull-out were firm rather than smooth on the first two entries, and the A/C was recovered 140 feet below the briefed recovery altitude, 9 knots from the target airspeed and 4 degrees from the entry heading. Marginal performance for the Training Section - these values sit near the upper edge of the desired band, and smoother handling in the pull-out is expected to consolidate the margin on the next sortie.

SP applied the Spin Prevention and Spin Recovery Procedures from memory without hesitation on every entry, confirming the direction of rotation correctly each time. Stick movements were smooth, solid and free of over-control, no secondary stall developed at any point, and the A/C limits were maintained with a wide margin. Recovery was achieved with negligible loss of altitude, level flight being regained within 30 feet of the briefed recovery altitude, within 2 knots of the target airspeed and within 1 degree of the entry heading. Accuracy and speed of execution were above the level expected of a student at this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.
